problem: Whether the variance alone, with no dependence on the number of summands or on the success probabilities, forces a lower bound on the normalized Turán deficit δ_k of a Poisson–binomial pmf near its mode, and in particular at the first descent index D.
debate: The literature on log-concavity, ultra-log-concavity and mode or mass-ratio bounds for Bernoulli sums: Hillion–Johnson, Johnson, Darroch, Pitman, Dümbgen–Wellner, and Bobkov–Marsiglietti–Melbourne.
gap: The known lower bounds on δ_k depend on n (the Hillion–Johnson ultra-log-concavity bound) or on the p_i (Johnson), and both degenerate when near-0 and near-1 summands pile up at fixed variance, while the mode-location and ratio results do not control δ_k at all.
contribution: A proof that Vδ_D ≥ 1/4 whenever V ≥ 1, a binomial family showing no constant above 1/3 is possible, consequences δ_k ≥ 1/(4V+|k−D|) at every index and 1/(4V+1) ≤ δ_c < 2/V at the rightmost mode, and a Haar-unitary example where the bound is of order 1/log N rather than 1/N, with the core one-variable inequality proved by computer in exact arithmetic.
note: The question is cleanly posed and placed against named prior work, but your first page never says what a probabilist gains from controlling δ_D beyond the Gaussian heuristic and one unitary-matrix example, and a constant left open between 1/4 and 1/3, with the key step proved by computer, will be pressed hard in review unless you show why the result matters.
